title: How Have U.S. Metro Home Prices Changed?
text: Over the past two decades, U.S. home values went through a boom, a crash, a slow recovery, and a pandemic surge. This page asks a simple question: how many metro areas have moved into “expensive” territory, and where did it happen?

title: How Have U.S. Metro Home Prices Changed?
text: Over the past two decades, U.S. home values went through a boom, a crash, a slow recovery, and a pandemic surge. This page asks a simple question: how many metro areas have moved into “expensive” territory, and where did it happen?

title: How Have U.S. Metro Home Prices Changed?
text:
The data
I use Zillow’s Home Value Index (ZHVI), which estimates the typical home value in each metro area each month. The data covers 90 metros from 2000 to 2026. I average each metro’s monthly values within a year and sort every metro-year into one of four price bands: under $200k, $200k to $400k, $400k to $600k, and over $600k. I call the top band “expensive.”

title: How Have U.S. Metro Home Prices Changed?
text:
1. The typical metro home

The typical metro home value rose from $129K to $363K. The shaded bands mark the housing bust and the pandemic boom, the two periods that shaped the rest of this story.

title: How Have U.S. Metro Home Prices Changed?
text:
2. A shifting mix

Each column adds up to 100% of metros. In 2000, 0% of metros were in the top band. By 2026, that share was 9%. Watching the orange layer grow, and the lighter blue layers shrink, is the clearest picture of the change in composition.

title: How Have U.S. Metro Home Prices Changed?
text:
3. How many metros crossed $600k

In raw counts, 0 metros were over $600k in 2000 and 8 were by 2026. Looking at the line, you can see when the group of expensive metros grew fastest, and whether the bust and the pandemic boom moved it.

title: How Have U.S. Metro Home Prices Changed?
text:
4. Where it happened

The rise of expensive metros was not even across the country. Lines are labeled directly at the end so you do not need a legend. By 2026, the West had the largest share of metros over $600k.

title: How Have U.S. Metro Home Prices Changed?
text:
5. The biggest movers

Overall, 90 of the 90 metros moved up at least one price band between 2000 and 2026. The chart shows the 12 metros that gained the most in dollars, and the color of the end point shows which band each one ended in.

title: How Have U.S. Metro Home Prices Changed?
section: 6. A caveat: where you draw the line matters
text:
6. A caveat: where you draw the line matters

The $600k line is my choice, and a different cutoff gives a different count. These values are also nominal dollars, so some of the move into higher bands reflects general inflation and not only real price growth. A cutoff of $400k tells a more crowded story than a cutoff of $800k, which is why I show all three here.

title: How Have U.S. Metro Home Prices Changed?
text:
Takeaways

The typical metro home value went from $129K in 2000 to $363K in 2026.
The share of metros in the expensive band rose from 0% to 9%, and 90 of 90 metros moved up at least one price band.
The West had the largest share of expensive metros in 2026, so the change was not even across regions.
The size of the “expensive” group depends on where you set the cutoff, and prices are not adjusted for inflation, so the results should be read as a pattern and not an exact count.
